newsitem.title: USA: Clinton "puzzled" by China fund-raising report.
newsitem.headline: Clinton "puzzled" by China fund-raising report.

text.p: President Bill Clinton knows nothing about a report that representatives of China might have sought to direct contributions from foreign sources to the Democratic Party, the White House said on Thursday.

The Washington Post on Thursday said a Justice Department probe into improper political fund-raising activities had uncovered evidence that the Chinese Embassy was used to plan contributions to the Democratic National Committee.

The Post said its sources declined to provide details about the scope of the evidence relating to the alleged efforts by Chinese representatives. They also declined to specify what foreign contributions might have been involved, but they said the new evidence was serious.
Deputy Attorney General Jamie Gorelick declined comment on the report.

Presidential Press Secretary Mike McCurry said he had showed the story to Clinton and he was "puzzled" by it. "But he was very concerned about it and expects that anything like that would be fully investigated."
McCurry said Clinton asked the White House legal counsel's office to contact Justice Department lawyers about the report.

McCurry also said he had talked with various officials about the story and "everyone I've checked with here at the White House doesn't seem to know anything about the news in this story, and I started checking from the top down."
"I'm having a hard time making heads or tails out of the story in the Washington Post," he said.

A Justice Department task force, consisting of 25 FBI agents and prosecutors from the department's public integrity section, is investigating questionable Democratic campaign fund raising, mainly involving foreign sources.

A focus has been on John Huang, a former Commerce Department official and DNC fund-raiser now at the centre of the controversy. About $1.5 million raised by him had to be returned because of questions about whether it came from foreign sources.

Another fund-raiser, longtime Clinton acquaintance Charles Yah Lin Trie, was a source of embarrassment when it was disclosed that he had used his influence to bring Wang Jun, head of a weapons trading company owned by the Chinese military, to a White House coffee meeting with Clinton.

One source quoted by the Post said the new dimension to the fund-raising investigation could result in Attorney General Janet Reno recommending that the matter be turned over to an independent counsel. But Gorelick denied the task force might be closer to seeking an independent counsel.

"The task force has standing instructions that if it finds any information that would lead it to believe that there should be an independent counsel they're to bring this to our attention immediately. And that has not occurred in this case," she said.

The Post said the Chinese Foreign Ministry had long urged the leadership in Beijing to increase its lobbying efforts in Washington, arguing that China had lagged behind Taiwan and Israel in trying to influence U.S. policy.

At the weekly Justice Department news briefing, Gorelick also declined comment on whether the investigation now covered former top White House aide Harold Ickes. The White House has denied that Ickes broke the law in discussing a $500,000 contribution to the Democratic National Committee in late October, right before the election.
